scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

prediction.raw: **YTA** (You're the Asshole) – **but with critical context**. Here's why: ### 🔍 **The Core Issue: How You Delivered the Reason, Not the Choice Itself** - **Your right to choose is unquestionable**: You absolutely have the right to wear any color for your wedding. No one (including your mother) gets to dictate your attire. That part is **not** YTA. - **But the *reason* you gave was cruel and unjustified**: - Saying *"your divorce is why I won’t wear white"* frames your mother’s marriage as a *failure* that "ruined" the tradition for you. This implies: - Her divorce is her fault (it rarely is). - Her marriage’s outcome should dictate your choices (it shouldn’t). - Her pain is a valid justification for your fashion preference (it isn’t). - This isn’t just insensitive—it’s **blaming her for your personal decision**. Divorce is complex, and it’s deeply unfair to reduce it to "she wore white, so it’s bad." Many divorced people wore white; many married people wore white. The color has no causal link to marital success. ### 💔 **Why This Was Especially Hurtful** - Your mother asked "why" out of care, not control. She likely wanted to understand *your* vision, not force her preferences. - When you said *"you’re the only woman in my family who broke the tradition and got divorced"*, you: - Turned her divorce into a punchline for your dress choice. - Ignored that she’s already hurt by the divorce (she said as much: "I tried my best..."). - Made her feel responsible for your discomfort. **That’s not okay.** ### 🌟 **What You Should’ve Done Instead** - **Keep the divorce out of it entirely**. Your reasons were valid without it: > *"I don’t like the white tradition—it’s modern, not ancient, and I prefer colors. My family’s colored dresses feel more authentic to us."* - If pressed for more, say: *"This is my personal style choice—it’s not about anyone else. I’d love to talk about colors we both like!"* - **Never weaponize a parent’s pain** to justify your decisions. That’s emotional manipulation, even if unintentional. ### ✅ **The Right Way Forward** - **Apologize specifically for the phrasing**: > *"Mom, I’m so sorry I said your divorce was the reason I don’t want white. That was unfair and hurtful—you didn’t cause my choice, and I should never have linked them. I just prefer colored dresses for my own reasons, and I know you meant well. I love you."* - **Reaffirm your autonomy**: > *"It’s my wedding, and I’ll choose what feels right for me—but I should’ve shared that without hurting you. I’m sorry for that."* ### 📌 **Key Takeaway** **Choosing a colored dress = perfectly reasonable.** **Using your mother’s divorce as justification = deeply hurtful and YTA.** You’re not the asshole for wanting color—but you *are* for weaponizing her pain to defend it. Fix that, and you’ll heal this. *(P.S. If you’re struggling to apologize, write it first—then say it. Her tears mean she’s hurting. Don’t let your frustration blind you to that.)*

Final thought: The user needs to apologize for the phrasing, not for choosing colored dress. The apology should focus on "I shouldn't have linked your divorce to my dress choice – that was unfair and hurtful." Because yes, that was cruel. The divorce isn't the mother's fault, and it's not the child's place to tie it to their wedding choices.
